name: Matriarchy
summary: As an ideology, matriarchy is the picture drawn by modern matriarchal studies of mother-centred, gender-egalitarian societies: clans traced through the mother, land worked communally with usage rights instead of private property, a gift economy, decisions by consensus, and a spirituality of the divine feminine. It is presented as a non-hierarchical order rather than rule by women over men. The sources say little on most of the test's questions about states, markets, war or law.
scope: The strand represented is modern matriarchal studies as defined by Heide Goettner-Abendroth (from 1988) and described in the field's reference pages: matriarchy as mother-centred, gender-egalitarian societies with a gift economy, matrilineal clans and consensus politics. Excluded are the popular and older anthropological senses of matriarchy as female rule or dominance, Bachofen's nineteenth-century 'mother right' stage theory, and the goddess-history writing of Gimbutas and Eisler (who prefer 'matristic'), none of which the defining sources adopt as their own definition. Answers rest on Goettner-Abendroth's own statement of the deep structure, not on the separate definitions of Sanday or Mann, and not on any society or feminist movement.

political-decisions-consensus.rationale: Goettner-Abendroth defines the political level of matriarchy by the principle of consensus, meaning unanimity on each decision.

minority-veto.rationale: Consensus is defined as unanimity regarding each decision, with one vote per person including the matriarch, so no decision binds a dissenting member without agreement.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Matters of the clan house are decided by its women and men in a consensus process in which no member is excluded, and village and regional bodies only carry those decisions back and forth.

decide-locally.rationale: Each decision is based in the individual clan house; delegates in village and regional councils do not decide but relay what the clan houses decided until consensus is reached.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Clan delegates meet in village and regional councils but do not make decisions themselves; they communicate those made in the clan houses until a consensus is reached.

natural-rulers.rationale: Matriarchies are defined as non-hierarchical, horizontal societies in which women guide their clans without ruling, the matriarch has one vote like everyone else, and no domination or classes develop.

property-fundamental.rationale: The economic level of matriarchy is defined as having no private property and no territorial claims, only usage rights on land and animals.

land-use-tenure.rationale: People simply have usage rights on the soil they till or the pastures their animals graze, with parcels given to each matri-clan and no private property or territorial claims.

collective-farming.rationale: Parcels of land and a number of animals are given to each matri-clan and worked on communally.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Goods held by the clan mother are distributed equally among her children and grandchildren, and clans' relative advantages are evened out by gift-giving at the festivals, so the economy is described as egalitarian and balanced.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Need-orientation is named as one of the maternal values and the clan mother is responsible for the sustenance of all clan members, though the sources speak of equal shares more than of need.

production-for-use.rationale: Matriarchies are said to foster subsistence economies in which a gift economy prevents an exchange economy built on accumulation.

local-production.rationale: Matriarchal economies are described as subsistence economies tied to the clan's own land and flocks, with exchange limited to gifts within the community.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Its model of society is small self-governing clan communities that work land communally and decide by consensus; the author presents this as a different model of life with present political relevance.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: In matriarchal culture divinity is immanent in the whole world, regarded as the Great Mother Nature, and society is built in her image.

god-not-male.rationale: Matriarchal societies are described as having no religions based on an omnipotent male God; the divine is feminine, the Great Mother or Goddess.

separate-church-state.rationale: The cultural level is defined by there being no separation between sacred and secular, so everyday and communal life carry ritual significance.

premarital-sex.rationale: The two genders are said to enjoy great freedom in their sexual lives, with visiting or walking marriage as one pattern.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Patriarchy is defined as domination by the fathers with hierarchical structures of domination, in contrast to matriarchal gender egalitarianism.

women-suffrage.rationale: Matriarchy is defined as gender-egalitarian: women and men decide together in the clan house, each with one vote, and no gender dominates the other.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Matriarchies are said to rest on maternal values (care, need-orientation, nonviolent conflict resolution) that permeate political practice, though the author says these values hold for everybody, not only women.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The clan's name, social status and political titles pass down through the mother's line, so inherited titles are part of the model.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: The field's own account faults European colonial Eurocentrism and the unilinear evolution theory with racist and sexist roots for distorting the study of non-Western matriarchal cultures.

missingStatements.text: The economy of a society should be based on gift-giving.
missingStatements.rationale: Goettner-Abendroth calls the gift economy the economic form of matriarchy and its field calls it a core concept of all matriarchies.

quotes.text: It is the economic manifestation of maternal values, which prevents development of an exchange economy with the accumulation of goods in the hand of the few.
Gift-economies, defined by modern Matriarchal Studies as a transitive relation in closed communities, is a core concept of all matriarchies.

missingStatements.text: Women should control the distribution of food.
missingStatements.rationale: The power of women over fields, flocks and food is what separates a matriarchy from a merely matrilineal society in Goettner-Abendroth's definition.

quotes.text: Most importantly, women have the power of disposition over goods and clan houses, and especially over the sources of nourishment: fields, flocks and food.
All these societies are characterized by matrilinearity, matrilocality, and women as keepers of the land and distributors of food, based on a structured gift economy.

missingStatements.declined: No current holder outside one theory.

notes: Themes searched: definition, economy, politics, kinship, religion, and the history of the term. The defining sources are a short conference paper, a field bibliography and a publisher summary; Goettner-Abendroth's full book (Peter Lang 2012) and Sanday's and Mann's books were not available open access, so government, law, war, foreign affairs, rights, technology and most ecology questions stay null. Sources about the popular sense (female rule) and the Amazon myth were not used for answers.
